newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil coffee council holds first official meeting.
newsitem.headline: Brazil coffee council holds first official meeting.

text.p: Brazil's new coffee council met formally for the first time in the capital of Espirito Santo state to discuss producer debt and how to maintain supply to the internal market, said the council's president, Industry and Commerce Minister Francisco Dornelles.
The council decided to put back the repayment deadline of producer debt by 90 days "so that we can examine and define a solution which will lead to a great stability in the sector," Dornelles said.

The 90 days will allow council members to examine a plan drawn up by producer representatives which was presented to the council today, said Gilson Ximenes, president of the National Coffee Council which represents growers.
In the plan, producers estimated their debt with Banco do Brasil was more than 400 million reais ($381 million) and they owed a further 100 million to private banks, Ximenes said.
The council, which is known as the Conselho Deliberativo da Politica do Cafe (CDPC), will next meet on April 28 in Belo Horizonte, the capital of Minas Gerais state.

The council also discussed how to maintain supply to the internal market and to meet external commitments by raising sales of government stocks, members said. Currently, monthly sales are limited to 200,000 60-kg bags.

"The auctions are carried out according to the necessities of the internal market. We have to increase the auctions," said Mauricio Assis, head of the primary commodities department at the Industry and Commerce Ministry.

The next auction -- scheduled to be held on March 5 -- will be slightly larger than 200,000 bags although a final total had not yet been set, Assis said. "We will raise it a little, it will be more than 200,000 bags," he said.
Both Assis and Dornelles stressed that auctions would not be held while the bulk of the new harvest was being brought in, which Assis estimated would be from July.

The council, which is comprised of six members of the private sector and six government representatives together with the president, is to be responsible for all aspects of Brazilian coffee policy from now on.
It will examine in coming months how to set up a forecasting system for the Brazilian crop, which Assis said would be in place by the next crop.
